issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: 'Being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma reminder for a female relief worker in a war zone, given the rest of the profile. The memory and appraisal items center on terror, self-blame, visibility/shame, and isolation, but nothing else suggests a women-specific interpersonal trauma cue. This trigger is therefore clinically hard to explain from the stated trauma context and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a maladaptive strategy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The profile otherwise emphasizes intrusive sensory reliving, terror on recall, avoidance of reminders, and emotion control. Gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is not impossible, but here it appears disconnected from the dominant memory-trigger-appraisal pattern and is not well linked to any other selected items.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a relief worker in a war zone, this appraisal is not impossible, but within this profile it is the least coherent item. The rest of the profile emphasizes sensory reliving, externally cued reminders, emotional control, suppression, and social alienation. 'Self-Blame' implies a specific moral/personal responsibility theme, but there are no accompanying memory, trigger, threat, or strategy items suggesting a personal action-based error or preventable mistake. In this configuration it stands out as insufficiently supported by the rest of the formulation compared with more externally focused appraisals.

vignette: Emma, a 52-year-old divorced North American woman and judge, has sought therapy after experiencing debilitating symptoms following her time as a relief worker in a war zone. The traumatic event she endured has left deep scars that continue to affect her daily life. On the anniversary of the incident, Emma is particularly vulnerable. The specific taste associated with the event—a blend of diesel fuel and burnt metal—often triggers intense memories. One day, while presiding over a case involving military personnel, she noticed one of them in full uniform, and was suddenly transported back to the war zone. She vividly heard the sound of gunfire and smelled the same acrid mix that had seared itself into her memory. Emma’s distress is exacerbated by the fact that these memories feel completely real. The auditory recall is particularly powerful; she hears the chaotic sounds as if they are happening in the present moment, which brings back the same terror she felt at the time. This full sensory reliving leaves her feeling vulnerable and isolated. She believes others can see what happened to her just by looking at her, and this belief has reinforced her sense of isolation. The memories often come when Emma is least prepared, such as during routine activities or in moments of quiet reflection. As a result, she tries hard to control her emotions and suppress thoughts about the trauma, but these efforts only serve to heighten her distress. She avoids circumstances that remind her of the event, such as being in dark environments, which further isolates her. Emma’s world has become a dangerous place. The memories have made her hyper-aware of potential threats, leading her to avoid not just specific triggers like uniforms and tastes but also broader scenarios where she might feel exposed or vulnerable. Her daily routine is punctuated by these avoidance behaviors, from skipping her favorite café because it smells faintly of diesel to avoiding crowded places. Her work as a judge has been affected by these avoidance strategies; she often passes on cases that involve military personnel or law enforcement officers, believing the memories will overwhelm her if she confronts them. This decision has strained her relationships with colleagues who do not understand why she declines certain cases. Emma is finally seeking help because she feels overwhelmed and exhausted from trying to manage her symptoms alone. Her most pressing fear is being unable to control her reactions in public or at work, where the stakes are high and any lapse could have significant consequences. She hopes therapy will provide her with tools to regain a sense of normalcy and reconnect with others without feeling constantly haunted by the past. The memory loop is tightening around Emma; each trigger brings back memories that amplify her negative appraisals, which in turn worsen her distress and reinforce her avoidance behaviors. This cycle leaves her feeling increasingly isolated and afraid. She hopes therapy will help break this vicious circle and allow her to reclaim her life without being constantly reminded of the war zone.
